method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar sits just below its highest since March 2025 because markets see a Federal Reserve rate rise on December 9 as all but certain, after hot core PCE inflation of 3.3% on Wednesday, November 25. It held steady in thin trading on Thursday, November 26, with US markets shut for Thanksgiving.

EUR.text: The euro sits near $1.09, close to its lowest since April 2025, because the Federal Reserve looks set to raise rates faster than the European Central Bank. On Thursday, November 26, notes from the ECB's October meeting backed a rate rise on December 17, and leaders calmly chose Pablo Hernández de Cos to run the bank from February 2027.

GBP.text: The pound sits near $1.31, close to its lowest in a year, as the dollar holds firm on bets of a Federal Reserve rate rise on December 9. Traders added to bets on Bank of England rises in December and February on Thursday, November 26, even though Governor Andrew Bailey said cheaper energy could mean a lower inflation peak.

JPY.text: The yen is a little firmer with the dollar near 159 yen, helped by Japan's warnings it may step in near 160 and by Bank of Japan rate-setter Naoki Tamura saying on Thursday, November 26 that rates may need to rise faster, backing a rise on December 18. Dearer oil is a cost for Japan. Tokyo prices come on Friday, November 27.

CHF.text: The Swiss franc rose to its strongest against the euro this month as falling AI shares and the Iran war sent money to safe places, and the Bank of England warned on Thursday, November 26 about AI debt. Against the dollar it slipped 0.4% that day, held back by bets on more Federal Reserve rate rises.

CAD.text: The Canadian dollar was the strongest major currency on Wednesday, November 25, bouncing from a 19-month low on bets of a Bank of Canada rate rise on December 9 after Governor Tiff Macklem said the bank was too slow on inflation after COVID. Brent oil rising 3.5% to about $94.60 a barrel adds support for this oil-exporting country's currency.

AUD.text: The Australian dollar edged back up to about 66.4 US cents on Thursday, November 26, after its lowest in a year, helped by the biggest jump in business investment since 2011 and inflation of 4.9% that keeps rates high. Falls in AI shares and proposed US tariffs on China and others still weigh.

NZD.text: The New Zealand dollar sits near 55 US cents, just above its lowest since 2009, after a 10-day slide stopped on Thursday, November 26. Markets now price a likely Reserve Bank of New Zealand rate rise to 3%, but US rates rising faster still pull money away.

XAU.text: Gold bounced to about $3,565 an ounce on Thursday, November 26, after falling to a 15-month low near $3,446 the day before. The bounce came in thin holiday trading, and a Federal Reserve rate rise on December 9 still looks all but certain, which weighs on a metal that pays no interest.

OIL.text: Brent crude rose for a third day to about $95.60 a barrel on Thursday, November 26, as Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed a strike on Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery and tankers kept hitting mines near the Strait of Hormuz. Worries about too much supply next year are the main brake ahead of the OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29.

items.headline: Brent crude climbs to $95.58 for a third day of gains before OPEC+ meets
items.story_title: Oil supply: surplus vs Gulf attacks
items.summary: Brent crude rose for a third straight day to about $95.60 a barrel by midday in London on Thursday, November 26, turning around an early dip.

beats.was: Brent fell from about $118 at the end of October to near $89 on Monday, November 23, as worries about too much supply in 2027 outweighed the Iran war. Yemen's Houthi rebels then claimed a drone strike on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery, the kingdom's largest.
beats.happened: January Brent traded about 1% higher at $95.58 around midday London time on Thursday, November 26, up from $89.37 on Monday, November 23. No loss of Saudi output or exports has been confirmed, and US crude stocks rose slightly in the week to November 20.
beats.means: Buyers still pay up for the risk of Gulf supply being hit, even without proof of lost barrels. Next year's supply glut is the brake, and the OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29 will set the tone for 2027 output.
beats.fx: Dearer oil helps the Canadian dollar and Norway's krone and is a cost for Japan and the euro area, which buy most of their energy abroad.

impact.why: A third day of gains on Gulf attack fears, though no Saudi supply loss is confirmed.
Higher oil prices lift income for Canada, a big oil exporter.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so dearer crude widens its import bill.

items.watch: The OPEC+ ministers' meeting on Sunday, November 29, and the expiry of January Brent on Monday, November 30.

items.headline: Dollar rally pauses for Thanksgiving
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The dollar held just below its highest since March 2025 on Thursday, November 26, as US markets shut for Thanksgiving, while the Swiss franc slipped 0.4% against it.

beats.was: The dollar has climbed for weeks as markets bet the Federal Reserve will raise rates by a quarter point on December 9 and again early in 2027. Hot core PCE inflation for October and a big upward revision to US growth in the third quarter, both out on Wednesday, November 25, added to those bets.
beats.happened: With US markets closed, the dollar index sat near 103.7. The euro was steady near $1.098 after its lowest since April 2025 earlier in the week, sterling was about $1.31 and the dollar near 159.25 yen. The franc weakened 0.4% to about 0.834 per dollar. One Mizuho strategist described the dollar's strength as defensive, after the US proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners on Wednesday, November 25.
beats.means: The holiday pause does not change the story: US rates look set to rise faster than elsewhere, which keeps money flowing to the dollar. Thin trading can make moves look bigger than they are until US markets reopen on Friday, November 27.
beats.fx: The dollar stays firm against most major currencies. The franc lost ground to the dollar on the day, even as it gained against the euro.

impact.why: Holds near its highest since March 2025 on bets of more Fed rate rises.
Slipped 0.4% against the dollar in quiet holiday trading.
Steady near $1.098, close to its lowest since April 2025.

items.watch: The return of US trading on Friday, November 27, and the Fed rate decision on Wednesday, December 9.

items.headline: EUR/CHF breakdown as safe-haven demand outweighs ECB–SNB rate repricing
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: The Swiss franc rose sharply against the euro in the week to Thursday, November 26, with the euro falling to about 0.907 francs before bouncing to near 0.915, as nervous investors sought a safe place for money.

beats.was: On Monday, November 23, a euro bought about 0.9485 Swiss francs. Since then the Nasdaq has fallen about 3.7% over a week on worries about AI stocks, South Korea's main share index has lost 7.4%, and Iran has tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
beats.happened: The euro broke below its November low of 0.9122 francs and touched 0.9070 before recovering to about 0.9153 by Thursday, November 26. The move came mostly from franc buying, since the euro was flat against the dollar. At the same time, the gap between expected European Central Bank and Swiss National Bank rate rises has narrowed, after Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% in October.
beats.means: Fear in markets is doing more for the franc than rate differences are. Both central banks are expected to raise rates in December, so the safe-place demand is the bigger driver for now.
beats.fx: The franc firms against the euro when shares fall and war worries grow, and softens again when calm returns. The Swiss National Bank decides on Thursday, December 10.

impact.why: Safe-place buying pushed the franc to its strongest against the euro this month.
Lost ground to the franc as stock markets fell, though steady against the dollar.

items.watch: The Swiss National Bank decision on Thursday, December 10, and the ECB decision on Thursday, December 17.

items.headline: Bank of England warns AI financing threatens financial stability, puts hyperscalers' exposure at over $4T
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: The Bank of England warned on Thursday, November 26 that borrowing to build AI is growing complex and hard to see into, putting the big tech firms' total exposure at just over $4 trillion.

beats.was: AI-linked shares make up just over half the value of the S&P 500, and they have fallen sharply since Monday, November 23 on worries about how the AI build-out is paid for. The Bank of England publishes a Financial Stability Report twice a year on risks to the financial system.
beats.happened: In its November report, the bank's Financial Policy Committee said AI funding is becoming circular and opaque, and that with higher interest rates several weak spots could give way at once. Bank staff put the potential exposure of firms such as Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle, including leases and guarantees, at just over $4 trillion. Borrowing by AI builders is almost double its 2025 level, and the cost of insuring some AI firms' debt against default hit records in the days before.
beats.means: A major central bank is now openly flagging AI debt as a risk to the wider system, which adds weight to the worries already hitting tech shares. It is a warning, not a policy change, so it does not alter UK rate plans.
beats.fx: Worries about AI debt tend to hurt currencies tied to global growth, like the Australian and New Zealand dollars, and help safe places like the yen and Swiss franc. Sterling itself barely reacts to the report.

impact.why: A central-bank warning on AI debt adds to the risk-off mood that weighs on growth-linked currencies.
More worry about markets tends to draw money to the franc.
A stability warning, not a rate signal, so little direct effect on the pound.

items.watch: How AI shares trade when US markets reopen on Friday, November 27, and the Bank of England rate decision on Thursday, December 17.

items.headline: Eurozone leaders back Hernández de Cos to succeed Lagarde at ECB
items.story_title: Will the ECB raise rates one last time in December?
items.summary: Euro area leaders chose Pablo Hernández de Cos, a former governor of Spain's central bank, on Thursday, November 26 to follow Christine Lagarde as European Central Bank president from February 2027.

beats.was: Christine Lagarde said on October 29 she will step down as European Central Bank president on February 7, 2027, before her term ends. The bank has raised rates twice this year, with euro area inflation at 4% in October, twice its 2% goal.
beats.happened: At a summit in Brussels, leaders backed Hernández de Cos, 55, who now runs the Bank for International Settlements and led the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024. He beat Klaas Knot, former head of the Dutch central bank, after the Netherlands dropped its objection. The same package names Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier to the bank's board. The choice still needs formal sign-off.
beats.means: The question of who leads the bank next year is settled without a fight. Some analysts see him as a little softer on inflation than Knot, but mainly as a pragmatic centrist, so no big shift in rate policy is expected.
beats.fx: A smooth handover removes a source of doubt for the euro. A slightly softer leader at the margin could trim rate-rise bets for 2027, but the December 17 decision is still the main driver.

impact.why: A calm, expected choice for the next ECB president, seen as a centrist, so little change to the rate path.

items.watch: Formal approval of the new ECB board, and the ECB rate decision on Thursday, December 17.

items.headline: Sterling steady as dollar takes a breather
items.story_title: Bank of England: how far do rates rise?
items.summary: The pound held near $1.31 on Thursday, November 26 after falling in 13 of the past 16 sessions, while traders added to bets on Bank of England rate rises in December and February.

beats.was: The pound has lost more than 2% against the dollar in November, back to levels last seen a year ago, as markets price a Federal Reserve rate rise on December 9. The Bank of England raised its rate to 4% earlier in November.
beats.happened: Sterling was little changed at about $1.31 and near 83.8 pence per euro in quiet holiday trading. Money markets now lean toward back-to-back Bank of England rises in December and February, and price three more rises by September 2027. A Santander Asset Management strategist said part of the pound's drop came from the fall in share prices, and that its longer-run value now looks better.
beats.means: UK rate bets are rising, which gives the pound a floor, but the dollar's own rate story has been stronger. The slide has paused rather than turned.
beats.fx: Firmer Bank of England bets are a mild support for the pound. The direction against the dollar still hangs on the Fed decision on December 9.

impact.why: Traders now lean toward two more Bank of England rate rises, in December and February.

items.watch: The Bank of England decision on Thursday, December 17, and the Fed decision on Wednesday, December 9.

items.headline: (ECB) Monetary policy accounts
items.story_title: Will the ECB raise rates one last time in December?
items.summary: Notes from the European Central Bank's October 28-29 meeting, published on Thursday, November 26, show many rate-setters could have backed a rate rise then, which supports the case for one on December 17.

beats.was: The European Central Bank raised rates in June and September, then held in October. Euro area inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, pushed up by dearer energy, while growth was slowing.
beats.happened: The written record of the October meeting showed many members said they could have supported a rise already. They worried that energy costs would spread into other prices, and noted the euro's slide against the dollar adds to import costs. They also saw growing risks to growth.
beats.means: The notes point to a rise at the December 17 meeting, which markets already expect. They add little new, but they show the bank's leaning has not softened.
beats.fx: Confirms a December rise that is mostly priced, a mild support for the euro. The bigger driver of the euro is still the gap with faster US rate rises.

impact.why: Many rate-setters were ready to raise rates in October, backing a December rise that is mostly priced.

items.watch: The ECB's decision and new forecasts on Thursday, December 17.

items.headline: European stocks rally as tech and banks rebound, tariff fears ease
items.story_title: New US tariffs
items.summary: European shares rose about 1.4% on Thursday, November 26, as tech and bank stocks bounced and proposed US tariffs on the EU looked likely to stay at the 15% rate agreed last year.

beats.was: On Wednesday, November 25 European shares fell more than 1% as US inflation came in hot, AI shares slid and the US proposed new import taxes on 14 trading partners, including the EU.
beats.happened: The STOXX 600 index of big European companies rose 1.4% early on Thursday, November 26. Chip and tech firms gained nearly 2%, and banks such as Deutsche Bank rose about 3%. Reports suggested US duties on EU goods will likely be capped at the 15% the two sides agreed last year.
beats.means: If the EU is spared a fresh jump in US import taxes, one risk to Europe's growth fades. Shares also followed Wall Street's late recovery from its AI sell-off.
beats.fx: Calmer trade news and firmer shares are a mild support for the euro and for currencies that track risk appetite, like the Australian dollar. US markets are shut for Thanksgiving, so moves are thin.

impact.why: US tariffs on the EU look likely to stay at the agreed 15%, easing a growth worry.
Stocks bounced after the AI sell-off, a better mood for risk-sensitive currencies.

items.watch: The final US tariff list, with written comments due by January 5, 2027.

items.headline: Oil Slides Despite Shipping Mine Claims and Supply Risks
items.story_title: Oil supply: surplus vs Gulf attacks
items.summary: Brent crude slipped below $94 a barrel by mid-morning in Europe on Thursday, November 26, giving back part of Wednesday's 3.5% jump even as Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed an attack on Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery.

beats.was: Brent rose 3.5% to $94.61 on Wednesday, November 25 after tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia spread. Oil is still about 13% lower than a month ago on worries about too much supply next year.
beats.happened: Brent fell about 0.9% to $93.79 by 0939 GMT on Thursday, November 26 and US crude dipped to about $83.33. The Houthis said they struck the Ras Tanura refinery, though Saudi Arabia and its state oil firm Aramco did not confirm it. Iran's army said a tanker hit a mine and caught fire in a closed-off area of the Strait. US crude stocks rose 1.1 million barrels last week.
beats.means: Attacks keep adding risk, but buyers took profits after a big jump, and plenty of supply caps prices. Analysts see Brent moving roughly between $88 and $97 for now.
beats.fx: A small dip after a big rise leaves oil-linked currencies like the Canadian dollar with most of their support. US markets are closed for Thanksgiving, so trading is light.

impact.why: Profit-taking after a 3.5% jump, while an unconfirmed Houthi refinery attack keeps supply risk alive.
Oil eased a little but held most of Wednesday's gains.

items.watch: The OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29 on output for 2027.

items.headline: Gold Price Today $3,565: Holiday Bounce From a 15-Month Low
items.story_title: Gold and Federal Reserve rate rises
items.summary: Gold traded near $3,565 an ounce early on Thursday, November 26, after bouncing back from a 15-month low of about $3,446 on Wednesday, November 25.

beats.was: Gold has fallen about 10% in November as hot US inflation made a Federal Reserve rate rise on December 9 look all but certain. Higher rates hurt a metal that pays no interest.
beats.happened: On Wednesday, November 25 gold dropped to about $3,446, its lowest since August 2025, then climbed back above $3,500 as traders who had bet on falls bought back before the US holiday. Early on Thursday, November 26 it was about $3,565, slightly lower on the day.
beats.means: The bounce looks like position-squaring in thin holiday trading, not a change in the story. Markets fully expect a December Fed rise and see another early in 2027.
beats.fx: Gold has steadied but still faces the pull of rising US rates. Central-bank buying stays a support underneath.

impact.why: A short-covering bounce from a 15-month low, while Fed rate rises still weigh.

items.watch: The Federal Reserve decision on Wednesday, December 9.

items.headline: Saudis down missiles targeting capital after Yemen port strikes
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Saudi Arabia said its air defences shot down two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh around midnight going into Thursday, November 26, after Saudi-led strikes on Yemen's Hodeidah port and Houthi attacks on the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan.

beats.was: Yemen's Houthi rebels, allied with Iran, have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia during the Iran war. They claimed a strike on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery on Wednesday, November 25, which Saudi officials have not confirmed, and a drone hit a Riyadh office tower on Tuesday, November 24, injuring 11.
beats.happened: An explosion was heard in Riyadh after an air-raid alert. The Saudi-led coalition said it also downed a cruise missile in the west and a drone near Jeddah port, with no civilian injuries. The Houthis said they hit Jeddah and Jazan in reply to coalition strikes on Hodeidah, Yemen's main port.
beats.means: The fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is widening, with the Saudi capital and Red Sea ports now targets. That adds a second risk to Gulf oil supply on top of tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.
beats.fx: More risk to Saudi supply keeps a floor under oil, which helps oil-exporting currencies like the Canadian dollar and supports safe places like the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Attacks reaching Saudi Arabia's capital and Red Sea ports raise the risk to Gulf supply.
Firmer oil supports the currency of a big oil exporter.
A wider Gulf conflict adds demand for safe places.

items.watch: The OPEC+ ministers' meeting on Sunday, November 29, which sets oil output for 2027.

items.headline: Australian dollar finds support in data centre boom, kiwi edges away from 17-year low
items.story_title: Australian inflation and the Reserve Bank of Australia
items.summary: Business investment in Australia jumped by the most since 2011 in July to September, driven by data centres, and the Australian dollar edged up to about 66.4 US cents on Thursday, November 26.

beats.was: The Australian dollar fell to its lowest in a year on Wednesday, November 25, near 65.6 US cents, and is down about 5.6% in November as AI shares slid and US rates looked set to rise. Inflation of 4.9% in October had already ruled out early rate cuts by the Reserve Bank of Australia.
beats.happened: Company spending on buildings and equipment rose far more than expected in the third quarter, led by data centres, though much of the money went on imported equipment. The Australian dollar rose 0.2%. The New Zealand dollar was flat near 54.9 US cents, ending a 10-day losing run just above its lowest since 2009.
beats.means: Strong investment points to an economy with more pace than feared, which backs the case that Australian rates stay high for longer. Markets do not expect a rate cut for many months. In New Zealand, swaps price about an 80% chance of a quarter-point rate rise to 3% at the next decision.
beats.fx: Better local news gives the Australian dollar some footing after a heavy month, though swings in AI shares still drive it day to day. The kiwi has stopped falling but has not turned.

impact.why: The biggest jump in business investment since 2011 supports keeping rates high.
A 10-day slide paused near a 17-year low, with a rate rise priced but not yet delivered.

items.watch: The Reserve Bank of Australia's last rate decision of the year in December.

items.headline: Dollar steady as sliding yields temper safe-haven bid
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The dollar held steady in Asian trading on Thursday, November 26, a little above a one-week low, as a drop in US bond yields took the edge off its pull as a safe place.

beats.was: The dollar index hit a 19-month high on Monday, November 23, after Nvidia's board put co-founder Jensen Huang back in charge and AI shares rallied. Hot US inflation figures on Wednesday, November 25 left markets almost sure the Federal Reserve will raise rates on December 9.
beats.happened: The dollar index sat flat near 103.7. The US 10-year bond yield fell as much as 0.1 point to about 4.8%, its lowest in two and a half months. The Australian dollar climbed back above 66 US cents after nearly a one-year low, and the euro held near $1.097.
beats.means: Lower US yields shrink the dollar's interest-rate edge, but markets still expect a Fed rate rise in December and another early in 2027. With US markets shut for Thanksgiving, trading is thin and moves can be jumpy.
beats.fx: The dollar is resting rather than turning. The yen, Swiss franc and Canadian dollar kept their gains from Wednesday, November 25.

impact.why: Falling bond yields offset firm bets on a Fed rate rise in December.
Back above 66 US cents after its weakest level in almost a year.
Held a 0.5% safe-place gain from Wednesday, November 25.

items.watch: The Federal Reserve's rate decision on December 9, which markets expect to be a quarter-point rise.

items.headline: Oil rises on supply concerns as Iran claims mine strikes on ships
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Brent crude edged up to about $94.70 a barrel early on Thursday, November 26, after Iranian state media said another oil tanker hit a sea mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz.

beats.was: Iran has tightened its control of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea route for about a fifth of the world's oil. Brent rose 3.5% on Wednesday, November 25 after Yemen's Houthi rebels said they attacked Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery, Ras Tanura.
beats.happened: Iran's Fars news agency, citing the Iranian army, said a tanker struck a mine and caught fire inside a zone Iran calls restricted. The claim was not confirmed by others. Brent rose 0.1% and US crude 0.4% to about $84 a barrel in quiet Asian trade.
beats.means: Each new attack claim adds to the risk that Gulf oil flows, which had begun to recover, get cut again. Against that, oil is still down nearly 20% in November on worries about too much supply next year.
beats.fx: Dearer oil helps oil exporters like Canada and is a cost for big importers like Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: An unconfirmed claim of another tanker hit by a mine in Hormuz.
Higher oil prices help Canada's export earnings.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so dearer crude is a cost.

items.watch: The OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29, where ministers set 2027 output, and whether other sources confirm the mine strike.

items.headline: BOJ's Tamura signals chance of faster-pace interest rate hikes
items.story_title: The yen, the Bank of Japan and intervention risk
items.summary: Naoki Tamura, one of the Bank of Japan's nine rate-setters, said on Thursday, November 26 the bank may need to raise rates faster if inflation runs too hot, and that a rise could come in December.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan raised its rate in June and September to 1.25%, then held in October. Markets widely expect a rise to 1.5% at the meeting ending December 18. Tamura is one of the two members most keen on higher rates.
beats.happened: Tamura said costlier raw materials from the Middle East conflict, a weak yen and strong demand linked to artificial intelligence are pushing prices up. He said the bank's rate is still some way below a level that neither helps nor holds back the economy.
beats.means: His words back a December rate rise and hint at more after it, but he is known for wanting higher rates, and he mostly confirmed what markets already expect. The dollar stayed near 159 yen.
beats.fx: Talk of faster Japanese rate rises gives the yen some support, though the gap with much higher US rates still holds it near its weakest levels.

impact.why: A rate-setter backs a December rise and hints at a faster pace after it.
Narrower rate gap with Japan over time, but the Fed is still raising too.

items.watch: Tokyo consumer prices on Friday, November 27, an early read on Japan's inflation before the December 18 decision.

items.headline: Asia shares bounce, AI and tariffs lurk in background
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: Asian shares rose modestly on Thursday, November 26 after Wall Street won back most of a deep fall. Japan's Nikkei gained 1.6% and South Korea's main index 1.9%.

beats.was: Asian chip-heavy markets had a rough November as doubts grew about the rally in artificial intelligence shares. Japan was down about 8% for the month, South Korea about 16% and Taiwan about 15%. The US also plans new tariffs on 14 big trading partners, including China, Japan and the euro area.
beats.happened: Buyers returned in Asia after US shares recovered late on Wednesday, November 25. Markets still price an almost certain Federal Reserve rate rise of a quarter point in December, and the US 10-year bond yield sat near 4.85%. Brent oil held near $94.80 and gold near $3,566, down almost 8% this month.
beats.means: The selling in tech shares has paused, but the tariff plan and doubts about AI firms have not gone away. US markets are shut for Thanksgiving, so trading is thin.
beats.fx: A calmer mood gives some relief to risk-linked currencies like the Australian and New Zealand dollars, while firm Fed rate bets keep the US dollar strong.

impact.why: Asian shares steadied, but tariffs on China still hang over Australia's biggest buyer.
A rebound in Tokyo shares cuts the need for the yen as a safe place.
Markets still see a Fed rate rise in December as all but certain.

items.watch: Whether chip shares hold the rebound when US markets reopen for a half-day on Friday, November 27.

items.headline: S&P may cut Nvidia's AA credit rating over board oversight after Huang's return
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: Ratings agency S&P Global warned on Wednesday, November 25 it may cut chipmaker Nvidia's AA credit rating by one step within 90 days, citing weak board oversight.

beats.was: Nvidia is the biggest company behind the stock rally built on artificial intelligence. Its boss Jensen Huang quit on November 12 over his personal conduct, and the board brought him back on Monday, November 23. Its debt has climbed to about $32 billion this year.
beats.happened: S&P put the rating on watch for a possible downgrade, pointing to the board's independence, the lack of a plan to replace Mr Huang and the firm's exposure to China. The cost of insuring Nvidia's debt against default hit a record, and its shares fell about 4% on the day.
beats.means: A one-step cut would still leave Nvidia with a strong rating, but the warning adds to doubts that have been dragging tech shares lower. Mr Huang faces questions from US lawmakers in early December.
beats.fx: Worries about the top AI firm weigh on the risk mood, which tends to hurt the Australian and New Zealand dollars and help the yen and Swiss franc.

impact.why: More doubt about the AI leader sours the mood in shares, which tends to drag the Aussie.
Nervous markets lean toward the yen as a safe place.

items.watch: Jensen Huang's hearings with US lawmakers on December 1 and December 3, and S&P's final decision.

items.headline: Stock Market Today Live, November 25, 2026: Stocks Win Back Most of Their Morning Losses After a Chip Sell-Off
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: US shares won back most of a deep morning slide on Wednesday, November 25. A fund that tracks the Nasdaq-100 ended down about 0.7% after being down more than 4% late in the morning.

beats.was: US tech shares had been falling for days, led by Nvidia, as doubts grew about the rally built on artificial intelligence. Hot inflation figures and a US plan for new tariffs on 14 economies added to the selling on the morning of Wednesday, November 25.
beats.happened: Buyers came back through the afternoon. The S&P 500 fund closed down about 0.3% and the Dow fund rose about 0.3%. Nvidia still ended about 4% lower and Micron about 4.5% lower. US markets are shut on Thursday, November 26 for Thanksgiving and close early on Friday, November 27.
beats.means: The panic of the morning eased, but chip shares are still under pressure. Thin holiday trading can make moves bigger in either direction.
beats.fx: A calmer close takes some heat off risk-linked currencies like the Australian and New Zealand dollars, and cools the rush into the yen.

impact.why: Shares recovered, but chip stocks still fell, so the risk mood is only half mended.
The kiwi gets some relief from the late rebound in shares.
Less panic means less need for the yen as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether chip shares steady when US trading resumes for a half-day on Friday, November 27.

items.headline: Forex — Day Close Report: Swiss franc and yen hold haven gains as dollar retreats
items.story_title: The Fed's next rate rise
items.summary: The dollar slipped about 0.2% against major currencies by the New York close on Wednesday, November 25, as US bond yields fell, while the Swiss franc and the yen kept their safe-place gains.

beats.was: The dollar had climbed near its highest in almost two years on bets that the Federal Reserve raises rates on December 9. Hot inflation and growth figures on the morning of Wednesday, November 25 backed those bets.
beats.happened: A deep but short-lived fall in tech shares sent money into US government bonds, pulling the 10-year yield down to about 4.85%. The euro edged up to near $1.10 and the dollar held near 159 yen.
beats.means: Markets still put the chance of a Fed rate rise on December 9 near 97%, so the dollar's dip reflects lower yields on the day, not a change in the rate outlook.
beats.fx: Lower US yields take a little support from the dollar. The franc and yen benefit when share markets wobble.

impact.why: Rate-rise bets hold, but falling bond yields pulled the dollar back a little.
The franc kept gains from the morning rush for safety.
The yen held its safe-place gains as US yields fell.
A softer dollar lifted the euro slightly.

items.watch: Thin trading on Thursday, November 26 with US markets shut, then Tokyo prices on Friday, November 27.

items.headline: Brent settles Wednesday at $94.61 and WTI at $83.68
items.story_title: Oil supply and prices
items.summary: Brent crude ended Wednesday, November 25 up 3.5% at $94.61 a barrel, and US crude rose 2% to $83.68, a second day of gains above 2%.

beats.was: Oil had sunk to its lowest since August on Monday, November 23 on hopes of US-Iran talks and worries about too much supply. Attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz then pushed it back up on Tuesday, November 24.
beats.happened: Yemen's Houthi rebels said they attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery and the financial district of Riyadh, raising fears for Gulf supply. Traders also bought back bets against oil before the US Thanksgiving holiday. US crude stocks rose 1.1 million barrels, a little less than expected.
beats.means: The risk of supply losses in the Gulf is back in the price after Monday's slump. The OPEC+ group of oil producers meets on Sunday, November 29 to set its output for 2027.
beats.fx: Higher oil tends to help the Canadian dollar and Norway's krone and to hurt big oil buyers like Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Attacks claimed on Saudi oil sites put a supply-risk premium back in prices.
Canada sells oil, so higher prices bring in more money.
Japan buys nearly all its oil abroad, so dearer oil costs it more.

items.watch: Whether the Houthi claims are confirmed by Saudi Arabia, and what OPEC+ decides on Sunday, November 29.

items.headline: Fed survey shows continued growth and sticky inflation in recent weeks
items.story_title: The Federal Reserve's rate rises
items.summary: The Federal Reserve's Beige Book, a survey of businesses across its 12 regions, found on Wednesday, November 25 that the US economy kept growing at a slight to moderate pace while price pressures stayed stubborn.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve's main rate sits at 3.75% to 4.00%, and markets expect it to raise that by at least a quarter point at its meeting on December 8 and 9. Earlier on Wednesday, November 25, core PCE inflation rose to 3.3%, its highest in three years.
beats.happened: Eight of the Fed's 12 regions reported slight to moderate growth and four saw no change. Jobs edged up and prices rose at a moderate pace, with firms pointing to energy, transport, healthcare, insurance and tariffs as costs that keep climbing. Many said they could not pass all of those costs on to customers.
beats.means: The survey gives the Fed no reason to back off a December rate rise: growth is holding and costs are still rising. Firms struggling to raise their own prices hints that some pressure may fade later.
beats.fx: It backs the case for a Fed rate rise, which keeps support under the dollar, though the sharp fall in US shares had already trimmed how many further rises markets expect.

impact.why: Steady growth and sticky prices keep a December Fed rate rise on track.
Higher US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.

items.watch: The Fed decision on Wednesday, December 9, and the US jobs report for November before it.

items.headline: Iran tightening control over Strait of Hormuz, spokesperson says
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's army said on Wednesday, November 25 that ships must arrange passage through the Strait of Hormuz with its forces, as the US sent a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, to the Gulf.

beats.was: The US-Iran war is close to nine months old and peace talks have stalled. The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea lane that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, has seen almost no traffic, and Iran says tankers under US escort hit mines there on Monday, November 23 and Tuesday, November 24.
beats.happened: Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akrami-Nia said the military is on high alert and ships must coordinate with Iranian forces to pass safely. The USS Theodore Roosevelt is joining two other US carriers already in the region.
beats.means: Both sides are adding force rather than talking, so the chance of the strait reopening soon looks lower and the risk of a clash at sea is higher.
beats.fx: A firmer standoff in the Gulf keeps oil supported and gives some lift to safe places like the Swiss franc, the yen and the US dollar.

impact.why: More warships and tighter Iranian control make a reopening of the strait less likely soon.
War risk brings some money into the franc as a safe place.
The dollar tends to gain when war fears rise.

items.watch: Whether more ships are hit, and whether any go-between country manages to restart US-Iran talks.

items.headline: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq sink on hot inflation, new Trump tariffs as chip rout continues
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: US shares fell hard on Wednesday, November 25, with the Nasdaq down about 4% and the S&P 500 down nearly 3% by late morning in New York, as chip stocks kept sliding and fresh inflation and tariff news hit.

beats.was: US tech shares had already dropped sharply on Tuesday, November 24, with Nvidia down 9%, ending a long rally built on artificial intelligence. Bringing back Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive on Monday, November 23 had briefly lifted shares.
beats.happened: Nvidia fell almost 9% more and an index of chipmakers lost over 6%. The Nasdaq-100 neared a fall of 20% from its peak, the usual line for a bear market. A gauge of expected share swings, the VIX, jumped about 28% to near 34. Core PCE inflation came in at 3.3% against 3.2% expected, and the US proposed new tariffs of up to 20% on 14 trading partners. Investors moved into US government bonds, pulling the 10-year yield down about 0.07 points to 4.82%.
beats.means: Markets are now dealing with two pressures at once: a sharp fall in the shares that drove the past rally, and a Federal Reserve still set to raise rates on December 9. Lower bond yields show some money already looking for safety.
beats.fx: A deep share sell-off tends to hurt risk-linked currencies like the Australian and New Zealand dollars and help the yen. Falling US yields take a little shine off the dollar's rate support.

impact.why: A deep fall in US shares drives money out of risk-linked currencies.
The kiwi tends to fall when share markets sell off hard.
Share market stress brings some money back to the yen.
Rate-rise bets hold, but US bond yields fell as investors sought safety.

items.watch: Whether the chip sell-off spreads further, and thin trading around the US Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday, November 26, with a half-day on Friday, November 27.

items.headline: USD/CAD Slips to 1.4240 as Hawkish BoC Outlook Bolsters Canadian Dollar
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: inflation and the rate path
items.summary: The Canadian dollar was the strongest major currency on Wednesday, November 25, up almost 1% against the US dollar to about C$1.424, a two-week high, as markets bet the Bank of Canada will raise rates again on December 9.

beats.was: On Monday, November 23 the US dollar bought about C$1.438, the Canadian dollar's weakest point in 19 months, because the Federal Reserve was expected to raise rates faster than the Bank of Canada. Governor Tiff Macklem said on Tuesday, November 24 the bank had been too slow to catch inflation after COVID, and that total inflation, not a core gauge, is what it targets.
beats.happened: Traders read Macklem's speech as a sign the bank will not wait, and moved to price a second straight quarter-point rise in December, taking the key rate to 2.75%. Canadian bond yields rose and the US dollar fell to about C$1.424. Canadian inflation has run near 3% since spring and is expected near 3.4% by year-end.
beats.means: The gap between US and Canadian rate paths is narrowing for the first time in weeks. That takes away some of the main reason the Canadian dollar had been sinking.
beats.fx: Higher expected Canadian rates support the Canadian dollar even while US rate-rise bets stay firm. Oil near $93 a barrel adds a little help.

impact.why: Markets now lean toward a Bank of Canada rate rise on December 9.
Fed rate-rise bets hold, but the dollar lost ground to the Canadian dollar.

items.watch: Canada's third-quarter growth figures on Monday, November 30, the jobs report on Friday, December 4, and the Bank of Canada decision on Wednesday, December 9.

items.headline: New Zealand Dollar rebounds from 2009 low ahead of confidence data
items.story_title: The kiwi and the RBNZ
items.summary: The New Zealand dollar bounced to just under 55 US cents by Wednesday, November 25, after ten straight daily falls took it to its lowest since March 2009 on Monday, November 23.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised markets on October 28 by holding its rate at 2.75% in a 4-3 vote, when a rise had been almost fully expected. US rates are higher and the Federal Reserve looks set to raise them again on December 9.
beats.happened: The kiwi won back about a quarter of its slide over two days, though it dipped near 54.5 cents on Wednesday, November 25 as tech shares fell across Asia, with South Korea's main index down over 6%. A New Zealand consumer confidence survey from ANZ and Roy Morgan comes on Thursday, November 26.
beats.means: The bounce is small next to the slide. The gap between New Zealand and US rates still pulls money away from the kiwi.
beats.fx: The kiwi stays weighed down by low local rates and by any fall in share markets, with short bounces when selling runs out.

impact.why: A small bounce from a 17-year low, but the rate gap with the US still weighs.

items.watch: The ANZ-Roy Morgan consumer confidence survey for November on Thursday, November 26.

items.headline: US economy grew much faster than first thought, new GDP count shows
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The US economy grew at a 4.3% yearly pace in July to September, well above the first count of 3.4% and the roughly 3.5% expected, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday, November 25.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve has been raising rates again because inflation is well above its 2% goal. The first count of US growth for July to September, published in October, showed a solid 3.4% yearly pace.
beats.happened: The second count lifted growth to 4.3%, an unusually large revision. Business spending on software and equipment, much of it tied to artificial intelligence, jumped, and household spending was revised up to a 4.2% pace from 3.8%. Company profits rose again.
beats.means: The US economy is running hot, not cooling, so there is little in the way of more Fed rate rises. Strong growth on top of firm inflation makes a December 9 rise look even safer.
beats.fx: Faster US growth backs higher US rates for longer, which supports the dollar against currencies whose central banks are moving more slowly. It also weighs on gold, which pays no interest.

impact.why: Growth revised up to 4.3% shows an economy strong enough to take more Fed rate rises.
A strong economy keeps US rates high, which makes gold less attractive.

items.watch: November jobs data in early December, the last big US report before the Fed meets on December 8-9.

items.headline: Fed's favored inflation gauge rose in October ahead of expected Fed rate hike next month
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: US core PCE inflation, the Federal Reserve's preferred gauge, rose to 3.3% in the year to October, a touch above the 3.2% expected, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday, November 25.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve has been raising rates again because inflation is well above its 2% goal, and markets saw a rise at its December 9 meeting as nearly certain. October PCE was the last big inflation report before that meeting.
beats.happened: Overall PCE prices rose 0.3% in October and 3.8% from a year earlier, as expected. Core prices, which leave out food and energy, also rose 0.3% on the month, and the yearly rate climbed to 3.3% from 3.1% in September. Personal income rose 0.7%.
beats.means: Underlying inflation is still speeding up, not slowing, so nothing here argues against a December rate rise. Betting markets kept the odds of a quarter-point rise near 94% after the report.
beats.fx: A slightly hot core reading backs the case for more Fed rate rises, which supports the dollar and weighs on gold, which pays no interest. The miss was small, so the bigger swing for markets on Wednesday, November 25 is still the slide in tech shares.

impact.why: Core inflation rising to 3.3% keeps a December 9 Fed rate rise firmly on track.
Higher US rates make gold, which pays nothing, less attractive.

items.watch: US markets are shut on Thursday, November 26 for Thanksgiving. The next big US report is November jobs data in early December, before the Fed meets on December 8-9.

items.headline: World reacts to Trump's new tariffs as US stocks tumble
items.story_title: New US tariffs on 14 trading partners
items.summary: China, the European Union and Switzerland rejected the US case for new tariffs on 14 trading partners on Wednesday, November 25, while US shares and gold fell hard the same day.

beats.was: The US Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump's broad global tariffs in February. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer then spent eight months investigating 14 economies over making more goods than their home markets can use.
beats.happened: The US proposed tariffs, highest at 20% on China, on 14 partners including the EU, Japan, India, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland. China's foreign ministry and the European Commission rejected the claim of excess production, and the Swiss government rejected it too. Norway, left off the list for now, welcomed the move.
beats.means: Trade partners are pushing back rather than offering deals, so the dispute may drag on while the tariffs are still only proposals. It lands on markets already shaken by a fall in tech shares.
beats.fx: Tariffs on China weigh most on currencies tied to Chinese demand, like the Australian and New Zealand dollars. The euro and Swiss franc face a direct hit to exports, though the franc can also draw safe-place money when markets are stressed.

impact.why: A 20% tariff on China threatens demand for Australian exports.
Trade fights and falling shares weigh on the kiwi.
The EU is on the list and rejected the case, so a trade fight looks likely.
Swiss exports are targeted, but market stress can bring money to the franc.

items.watch: Whether any of the 14 economies opens talks or answers with tariffs of its own before the US makes the rates final.

items.headline: BoE's Bailey sees lower inflation peak if energy prices stabilise
items.story_title: Bank of England: how far do rates rise?
items.summary: Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey told UK lawmakers on Wednesday, November 25 that inflation would peak lower than forecast if energy prices hold where they are, while two colleagues sounded more worried about prices.

beats.was: The Bank of England raised its rate to 4% earlier in November and forecast on November 5 that UK inflation would peak near 5% in mid-2027. Oil and gas prices have eased since then, and markets lean toward another rise on December 17.
beats.happened: At a hearing of Parliament's Treasury Committee, Bailey said the inflation peak would be lower if energy prices stay at current levels, though he noted the economy has held up better and job market slack has stopped growing. Policymaker Catherine Mann said the bank should raise rates more and sooner. Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli said she is less sure that underlying price pressure is still easing, and expects food inflation near 5% next year.
beats.means: The bank's leaders are not of one mind: the governor sees some relief from cheaper energy, while others see sticky prices that need more rate rises. That leaves the December 17 decision more open than the most hawkish voices suggest.
beats.fx: Mixed signals for the pound: Bailey's softer tone trims rate-rise bets a little, while Mann and Lombardelli keep the case for more rises alive.

impact.why: The governor sees a lower inflation peak, but two colleagues lean toward more rate rises.

items.watch: The Bank of England decision on December 17, and UK energy prices into January.

items.headline: Oil Jumps Over 2% as Saudi Arabia Downs Drones Over Ras Tanura
items.story_title: Oil supply: surplus vs Gulf attacks
items.summary: Brent crude rose more than 2% to about $93.60 a barrel by mid-morning in New York on Wednesday, November 25, after Yemen's Houthi rebels said they struck Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery.

beats.was: Ras Tanura is Saudi Arabia's largest refinery and sits beside a terminal that can load about 6.5 million barrels of oil a day. A drone attack shut it in March, and it took about four months to restart. Brent had slipped to near $90 on fears of too much oil next year.
beats.happened: Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group hit the refinery and set off fires. The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses destroyed four drones over the site but did not say whether the refinery was damaged, and the claim has not been confirmed. Brent climbed about $2.20 and US crude about $1.50, helped by traders closing bets on lower prices before the US Thanksgiving holiday.
beats.means: Even an unconfirmed hit on a key Saudi site puts some war risk back into oil, on top of Iran's mine claims in the Strait of Hormuz. Talk of a supply surplus next year still caps how far prices run.
beats.fx: Firmer oil supports the Canadian dollar, while more Gulf fighting adds a little safe-place demand for the Swiss franc.

impact.why: A claimed strike on Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery lifted Brent more than 2%.
Higher oil prices help Canada's export earnings.
Wider Gulf fighting draws some money to safe places.

items.watch: Whether Saudi Arabia or the oil company Aramco confirms any damage, and the OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29.

items.headline: Gold slides below $3,500 amid Fed rate hike expectations, AI stock rout
items.story_title: Gold and Federal Reserve rate rises
items.summary: Gold fell below $3,500 an ounce on the morning of Wednesday, November 25, its lowest since September 2025, after US inflation figures kept a Federal Reserve rate rise in December all but certain.

beats.was: Gold has been sliding for two months because the Federal Reserve is raising rates, which makes a metal that pays no interest less attractive. It held just above $3,500 on Friday, November 20, a level many saw as a floor.
beats.happened: US PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred price gauge, came in at 3.8% for the year to October, as expected, with the core measure a touch above forecasts. Spot gold then dropped close to 3% and US gold futures fell to about $3,457. Futures pricing puts the chance of a quarter-point Fed rise on December 9 at about 96%, and New York Fed President John Williams said stubborn inflation points to tighter policy. Silver lost close to 4%.
beats.means: The $3,500 floor has given way, so gold is now trading at levels last seen more than a year ago. Some analysts also point to investors selling gold to raise cash as tech shares fall.
beats.fx: Gold moves against the dollar and US yields, so this drop mirrors how firmly markets expect the Fed to keep raising rates.

impact.why: A break below $3,500 to its lowest since September 2025.
Near-certain Fed rate-rise bets keep the dollar firm.

items.watch: The Federal Reserve decision on Wednesday, December 9.

items.source: Office of the US Trade Representative
items.headline: USTR Makes Determinations and Proposes Actions in 14 Section 301 Investigations Relating to Structural Excess Capacity
items.story_title: New US tariffs
items.summary: US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer proposed new import taxes on 14 economies, including China, the European Union, Japan and Switzerland, after a probe into excess factory output, his office said on Wednesday, November 25.

beats.was: The US Supreme Court struck down many of President Trump's tariffs in February, so the White House turned to a different trade law to tax imports. A probe into whether trade partners make far more goods than they need was expected to bring new duties.
beats.happened: The probe found 14 economies at fault. Proposed rates are up to 15% for the EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland, up to 20% extra for China on most goods, up to 25% for India and up to 35% for Vietnam. Mexico and Norway were spared. The rates are only proposals: comments are due January 5, 2027 and hearings follow on January 25.
beats.means: For the biggest partners the rates match caps already in their trade deals, so the news is less harsh than feared. China and parts of Southeast Asia take the bigger hit, and nothing changes until early 2027 at the soonest.
beats.fx: New tariffs weigh on currencies tied to world trade and China, like the Australian dollar. The euro, yen and franc face only small direct effects because their rates stay near existing caps.

impact.why: An extra 20% on Chinese goods hurts Australia's biggest customer.
The EU is named, though its 15% rate matches its trade-deal cap.
Japan is named at up to 15%, but trade worries also bring some money back to the yen.
Switzerland is named at up to 15%, while trade worries add some safe-place demand.

items.watch: Public comments on the proposed tariffs are due January 5, 2027, with hearings on January 25.

items.headline: Iran says ships hit mines in Hormuz, warns vessels to coordinate passage
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy said on Wednesday, November 25 that two oil tankers hit mines, exploded and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz while using a route Iran had not approved.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the sea lane for about a fifth of the world's oil, has been fought over since the US-Iran war began, and the US is blockading Iranian ports. Several ships have been hit near the strait in recent days.
beats.happened: Iran said two tankers struck mines and burned after taking an unapproved route. An Iranian army spokesman said new systems now watch the strait and that ships not working with Iranian forces face more danger. Tehran told Washington it will not let shipping return to normal until its demands are met, including an end to the US blockade.
beats.means: Iran is pressing its claim to control who passes through Hormuz, which keeps a risk premium in oil. Through Qatari go-betweens it has said it would reopen the strait within 48 hours if its conditions are met, so a deal remains possible.
beats.fx: Each new attack props up oil prices, which supports the Canadian dollar, and adds safe-place demand for the Swiss franc and gold.

impact.why: Mines and burning tankers raise the risk of losing Gulf supply.
War escalation draws money to safe places.
Higher oil prices help Canada's export earnings.

items.watch: Any word through Qatar on talks to reopen the strait, and the OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29.

items.headline: Nasdaq futures slide over 2% on fresh US tariff concerns; inflation data in focus
items.story_title: The AI share sell-off
items.summary: Nasdaq 100 futures fell about 2.2% early on Wednesday, November 25, with Nvidia down nearly 5% before the open, as reports of new US tariffs added to a slide in chip stocks.

beats.was: US tech shares have fallen hard this month, and the Nasdaq and S&P 500 are on track for their worst November since 2008. Nvidia's board put Jensen Huang back in charge as chief executive on Monday, November 23, which briefly lifted shares.
beats.happened: By 4:32 a.m. New York time, Nasdaq 100 futures were down about 2.2%, S&P 500 futures 1.3% and Dow futures 0.75%. Chipmakers Micron, AMD and Marvell fell more than 5% before the open, and Dell fell 6% even after raising its forecasts. Reports of new tariffs on 16 trading partners added to the selling.
beats.means: Another leg down in tech shares, now with trade worries on top, weighs on risk appetite worldwide. Futures pricing still shows about a 97% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates on December 9 and 63% for another rise in January, so falling shares have not changed rate bets yet.
beats.fx: Falling shares usually weigh on risk-linked currencies such as the Australian and New Zealand dollars and help the Swiss franc and yen. October PCE inflation and third-quarter GDP, out at 8:30 a.m. New York time on Wednesday, November 25, will steer the dollar.

impact.why: A deeper slide in tech shares cuts risk appetite, which the Aussie tracks closely.
The kiwi, already at a 17-year low, also suffers when shares fall.
Selling in shares tends to bring some money back to the yen.

items.watch: US October PCE inflation and third-quarter GDP at 8:30 a.m. New York time on Wednesday, November 25. US markets are shut on Thursday, November 26 for Thanksgiving.

items.headline: Trump administration set to unveil new tariffs, sources say
items.story_title: New US tariffs
items.summary: The Trump administration is close to releasing a probe into spare factory capacity in 16 trading partners, which is expected to bring new import taxes, three sources told Reuters on Wednesday, November 25.

beats.was: The US Supreme Court struck down many of President Trump's tariffs in February, and the White House has since been looking for other legal routes to tax imports. Trade deals cap US tariffs at 15% for the European Union, Japan and South Korea, and at 20% for China if a truce ending January 10 is extended.
beats.happened: Sources say the probe into excess production is about to be published, with new duties set country by country and stacked on top of existing ones. A trade lawyer expects rates between 15% and 25%. Mexico and Norway are unlikely to face them right away. The Wall Street Journal said results could come before the end of the week of November 23.
beats.means: A fresh round of tariffs adds to costs for US importers and hurts exporters abroad, just as markets were already nervous about tech shares. Staying under the trade-deal caps limits the damage for the biggest partners.
beats.fx: Tariff worries tend to hit currencies tied to global trade and risk appetite, like the Australian and New Zealand dollars, and to help safe places like the Swiss franc.

impact.why: New tariffs on major trade partners hurt global trade and risk appetite, which the Aussie tracks.
The EU is among the likely targets, though its 15% cap should hold.
Trade worries add to demand for a safe place to park money.

items.watch: The release of the US probe into excess industrial capacity, which the Wall Street Journal said could come before Sunday, November 29.

items.headline: Australia CPI Surges to 4.9% as Underlying Inflation Accelerates to 3.8%
items.story_title: Australian inflation and the Reserve Bank of Australia
items.summary: Australian prices rose 4.9% in the year to October, up from 4.3% in September and a little above forecasts, Australia's statistics office said on Wednesday, November 25. The trimmed mean, a gauge that strips out the biggest swings, rose to 3.8%.

beats.was: Australian inflation was already well above the Reserve Bank of Australia's 2-3% target, while jobs have been falling and business activity shrinking. Economists expected October's yearly rate near 4.7-4.8% and the trimmed mean to hold at 3.6%.
beats.happened: Yearly inflation jumped to 4.9%, its highest in about three years. Electricity costs rose about 25% from a year earlier as government power rebates ran out, and housing and fuel costs also climbed. The trimmed mean rose to 3.8% from 3.6%, so price pressure is spreading beyond a few items.
beats.means: Underlying inflation moving up, not just one-off power bills, makes it much harder for the Reserve Bank of Australia to ease even as the job market weakens. Most big-bank economists still expect it to hold rates at its December 7-8 meeting.
beats.fx: Hotter inflation props up Australian interest rate expectations, which supports the Australian dollar after weeks near its lows.

impact.why: Inflation beat forecasts and the underlying gauge rose, keeping rate cuts off the table.
The kiwi often moves with the Australian dollar on Australian news.

items.watch: US October PCE inflation later on Wednesday, November 25, and the Reserve Bank of Australia decision on Tuesday, December 8.

items.headline: Stock Market Today, Nov. 24: Tech Sell-Off Drags Nasdaq as Dow Gains on Value Rotation
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: US tech shares fell again on Tuesday, November 24, with the Nasdaq down 1.5% and Nvidia down about 6%, but the Dow rose almost 1% as money moved into health care and retailers. Gold ended about 2.7% lower near $3,554.

beats.was: US shares had their best day since April 2025 on Monday, November 23, after chip maker Nvidia put Jensen Huang back in charge and its stock jumped about 31%.
beats.happened: At the New York close the Nasdaq lost 1.5% and the S&P 500 0.5%, while the Dow gained 0.85% to just above 50,000. Nvidia gave back about 6%, and other chip and tech names fell harder. Health care and retailers such as Kohl's and Dollar Tree rose after strong results, and a jump in US consumer confidence helped. The US 10-year yield held at 4.92%, and gold fell about 2.7%.
beats.means: Investors are pulling back from the AI trade but not from the US economy, so this looks more like a shift between sectors than a broad loss of nerve. Steady yields near 5% keep the cost of holding gold high.
beats.fx: Weaker tech shares weigh a little on the Australian and New Zealand dollars, while a confident US economy and high yields support the dollar and press on gold.

impact.why: Gold lost about 2.7% with US 10-year yields near 5%.
Another tech sell-off cools appetite for risk-linked currencies.
The kiwi near a 17-year low stays exposed when tech shares slip.
Shares outside tech rose on a confident US consumer.

items.watch: US October PCE inflation, the Federal Reserve's preferred price gauge, on Wednesday, November 25.

items.headline: Iran says 3 oil tankers hit underwater mines despite US naval escort
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say three oil tankers sailing under US protection hit underwater mines near the Strait of Hormuz, and on Tuesday, November 24 claimed a fourth caught fire. The US answered with new sanctions on Iran's money networks.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran on February 28, and a deal signed in June has stalled over shipping. The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, still sees far fewer ships than before the war, and the US now escorts tankers through it.
beats.happened: The naval arm of Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three escorted tankers struck mines, one off Iran's southern coast and two in the eastern part of the strait, and that US air cover failed to stop it. On Tuesday, November 24 it said a fourth tanker caught fire after hitting a mine east of the strait. No names or damage details were given and the claims are not confirmed. The US Treasury put sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses and front companies, and a third US aircraft carrier joined two already in the Gulf.
beats.means: If mines are now in the water, US escorts are not enough to make the route safe, which raises the risk of a sudden cut to Gulf oil. More carriers and sanctions show the US digging in rather than easing off.
beats.fx: A riskier sea lane props up oil prices and with them the Canadian dollar, and keeps some safe-place demand for the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Mines in the strait would make even escorted tankers unsafe.
A tougher US stance and more attacks keep safe-place demand alive.
Firmer oil prices help Canada, a big oil exporter.

items.watch: Whether shipping groups or the UK's maritime agency confirm mine strikes, and the OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29.

items.source: The Conference Board via PR Newswire
items.headline: US Consumer Confidence Surged in November
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: US consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 in November, far above the 92.5 expected and its best since January 2025, as people felt better about finding work.

beats.was: Markets already treat a Federal Reserve rate rise on December 9 as close to certain, and the dollar sits near its highest since March 2025. The Conference Board's monthly survey of US households had read 91.9 in October.
beats.happened: The Conference Board said on Tuesday, November 24 that its index rose more than 11 points to 103.3. Views of current conditions and of the months ahead both improved, more people said jobs were easy to find, and the share expecting to cut back on hiring fell. Households' expected inflation for the next year stayed high at 5.7%. The group linked part of the lift to less uncertainty after the midterm elections.
beats.means: Confident households tend to keep spending, which supports the case that the US economy can take higher rates and gives the Fed less reason to pause.
beats.fx: A stronger US consumer adds support to the dollar against most currencies, and weighs most on the yen and the euro, where rates are lower.

impact.why: A big upside surprise in household mood backs more Fed rate rises.
Firmer US rate bets widen the gap with Japan's low rates.
Adds to the view that the Fed will keep raising rates faster than the European Central Bank.

items.watch: US October PCE inflation on Wednesday, November 25, the Fed's preferred price gauge.

items.headline: Bank of England's Greene says UK needs faster rate hikes
items.story_title: Bank of England: how far do rates rise?
items.summary: Bank of England policymaker Megan Greene said on Tuesday, November 24 that the bank is a little behind on inflation and should raise rates faster if the Middle East conflict drags on.

beats.was: The Bank of England raised rates earlier in November for the first time in three years, as the conflict with Iran pushed up energy costs. UK household energy bills are expected to jump about 26% in January.
beats.happened: Greene, one of the nine members who vote on UK rates, told a London business meeting that the bank is slightly behind where it should be and that the chance of a lasting peace deal in the Middle East looks very low. She said the UK should tighten faster if the conflict continues. Markets price about an 80% chance of another quarter-point rise on December 17.
beats.means: A voting member openly asking for faster rises makes a December move look more likely, and raises the chance that UK rates keep climbing into 2027 if energy prices stay high.
beats.fx: Firmer rate-rise bets give the pound some support near its 19-month low against the dollar, which still has its own strong rate story.

impact.why: A rate-setter calling for faster rises firms bets on a December 17 Bank of England move.

items.watch: The Bank of England decision on December 17, and UK energy prices into January.
